summary: Defines how the Alternate-Marking method is carried in IPv6 packets. It specifies an extension header option that can sit in either the Hop-by-Hop Options header or the Destination Options header, so network operators can passively measure loss and delay inside an IPv6 domain.

eli5.summary: IPv6 packets get a small sticker that says red or blue. Routers along the way read the sticker to count packets and see whether any were lost or slow.

questions: ipv6 hop-by-hop option for performance measurement
how to measure ipv6 packet loss
what is the altmark ipv6 option
how does alternate marking measure packet loss
subtitle: An IPv6 option that carries Alternate-Marking bits so networks can passively measure packet loss and delay on live traffic.

tldr.problem: The Alternate-Marking Method can measure loss, delay and jitter on live traffic, but it needs a marking field in the packets. IPv6 had no agreed place to put one.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9343 defines the AltMark option, a TLV for the IPv6 Hop-by-Hop or Destination Options header. It carries a 20-bit FlowMonID plus an L (loss) bit and a D (delay) bit, written only by the source node.
tldr.outcome: Operators inside a controlled domain can measure loss and delay hop by hop or end to end. The RFC requires deployment only in a controlled domain, because outsiders could otherwise inject or tamper with the option.

today: RFC 9343 is a Proposed Standard, published in December 2022, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the method described in RFC 9341 and RFC 9342.

sections.title: Alternate Marking on IPv6
sections.content:
RFC 9341 and RFC 9342 describe a passive performance measurement method that can measure packet loss, latency and jitter on live traffic. It is called the Alternate-Marking Method because it marks consecutive batches of packets by switching the value of a marking bit.

RFC 9343 defines how to use the method in IPv6. It introduces a TLV (type-length-value) that can be encoded in the Hop-by-Hop or Destination Options headers of RFC 8200. The goal is detailed loss, delay and delay variation measurements, hop by hop and end to end, to locate problems exactly in an IPv6 network.

The method MUST be applied to IPv6 only in a controlled environment.
sections.eli5: This RFC says where on an IPv6 packet to put the red-or-blue sticker so routers can use it to count packets and find trouble.

sections.title: Where to Put the Marking
sections.content:
The RFC weighs the alternatives for a marking field. Reusing an existing extension header leads to a non-optimized implementation, encoding the marking in the destination address is very expensive, and using the Flow Label conflicts with its use for load distribution (RFC 6438). It concludes that a Hop-by-Hop or Destination Option is the best choice.

Only the source node writes the option. Intermediate and destination nodes MUST only read it. A Hop-by-Hop option is not inserted or deleted on the path, but any node may read it, and nodes only measure if configured to. A Destination option is not processed by nodes on the path until the packet reaches the destination, except that if there is a Routing Header, any visited destination in the route list can process it.

The RFC admits that in real implementations, packets with a Hop-by-Hop option may be skipped or sent to a slow path. It treats that as a general problem outside its scope.
sections.eli5: The sticker goes in a special pocket in the packet's header. Only the first router writes on it, and everyone else just reads it.

sections.title: The AltMark Option
sections.content:
The AltMark option is a TLV with an 8-bit Option Type and an Opt Data Len of 4. The data holds a 20-bit unsigned FlowMonID (flow monitoring identifier), an L flag for loss measurement, a D flag for single-packet delay measurement, and reserved bits that MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt.

The three high-order bits of the Option Type are set to 000. The first two bits mean 'skip over this option and continue' if a node does not recognize it, and the third means the option data does not change en route. The FlowMonID MUST be set pseudo-randomly by the source node or by a centralized controller.

IANA allocated the option type value 0x12 (binary 00 0 10010) in the Destination Options and Hop-by-Hop Options registry, named AltMark.
sections.eli5: The sticker has a flow number, a loss switch and a delay switch. The first router sets them and nobody else is allowed to change them.

sections.title: Measuring Loss and Delay
sections.content:
For loss, the source groups a flow into batches and sets the L bit to the same value for all packets in a batch, switching between 0 and 1 after a fixed number of packets or on a fixed timer. Nodes along the path count packets per batch. Comparing counts between nodes shows loss in any single batch between any two nodes. Timer-based batches are preferable because they are more deterministic.

Clocks matter. Ignoring network delay, node clocks MUST be synchronized to the same reference with an accuracy of +/- B/2 time units, where B is the batch duration, and batches must be long enough to cope with clock error and reordering.

For delay, there are two options. With single marking, only the L bit is used (D MUST be zero) and the time a new batch starts is compared between nodes, which is accurate only if there is no loss or reordering at batch edges. With double marking, the D bit additionally marks selected packets so their timestamps can be compared per packet. The most efficient mode is one double-marked packet per batch, and the RFC prefers double marking. The method can also measure inter-arrival jitter.
sections.eli5: The colors switch on a timer, so every router can count how many packets of each color it saw. If one router counted fewer, packets were lost between them. A special marked packet can also be timed to see how slow the trip was.

sections.title: Flow Identification with FlowMonID
sections.content:
The FlowMonID names the monitored flow. It reduces per-node configuration (no ACL per flow), simplifies counter handling, and eases export and correlation at collectors. It is different from the IPv6 Flow Label, which may be changed en route and whose reuse could change forwarding behavior, so the two are disjoint.

With 20 bits, pseudo-random choice can collide. By the birthday problem the RFC gives a 50% collision chance at 1206 flows, so it is RECOMMENDED to combine the FlowMonID with source and destination addresses. That allows 145 concurrent flows per host pair at a 1% collision chance with pseudo-random values, or 1048576 with a centralized controller that guarantees uniqueness.

Deployments MUST use a consistent identification approach, and nodes SHOULD all use the same mode. Section 5.4 notes the method extends to multipoint flows through the clustered method of RFC 9342, where the FlowMonID can identify a multipoint-to-multipoint flow.
sections.eli5: Each flow gets a number so routers know which flow a sticker belongs to. Two flows might pick the same number by luck, so the RFC suggests also looking at who is sending and receiving.

sections.title: Controlled Domains Only
sections.content:
The IPv6 application of Alternate Marking MUST be deployed in a controlled domain: a managed network that selects, monitors and controls access, and enforces policy at its boundaries. It may span multiple administrative domains, in which case the RFC RECOMMENDS joining them with IPsec or another VPN technology that gives full confidentiality and integrity protection.

Typically this means an overlay network where user traffic is encapsulated at one border with the relevant extension header and decapsulated at the other. An implementation MUST filter packets that carry Alternate-Marking data when entering or leaving the domain. Customer Premises Equipment or Provider Edge routers are the likely start and end nodes, while user equipment can be one only if fully managed.
sections.eli5: The stickers are only meant for a private club of routers run by people who trust each other. Packets with stickers must not be allowed in or out.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The RFC separates harm caused by the measurement from harm to the measurement. The option must not alter the quality of service of packets. An on-path attacker could alter flags, or insert or delete the option, to fake loss or delay, hide real problems, or trigger needless operator action. Packets from outside the domain could waste router resources, which is mitigated by filtering at the boundary. If marking is not supported in the domain, an outside option is treated as an unrecognized option, with the only effect being 48 bits of extra packet size.

On privacy, the option holds no user data, but the FlowMonID is more sensitive because it can allow flow tracking and path reconnaissance. The marking bits alone reveal little from a single monitoring point. Configuration of the option MUST be secured, and channels reporting flow statistics MUST be secured.

The method relies on time synchronization, so attacking the time protocol or time source (for example by GPS spoofing) can compromise measurement integrity. The RFC points to RFC 7384 and Network Time Security (RFC 8915).
sections.eli5: A sneaky stranger could change stickers to make routers think packets are being lost, or follow the flow numbers to spy. Keeping the stickers inside a locked club and checking the doors is the fix.

items.title: Hop-by-Hop Option
items.text: Every router on the path with the feature enabled.

items.title: Destination Option, no Routing Header before it
items.text: Only the node in the Destination Address.

items.title: Destination Option before a Routing Header
items.text: Every destination node in the route list.
